web.title: Your family income estimate for family assistance payments
web.description:
## Phone us
### Centrelink families line
Use this line if you need help with family payments, such as Family Tax Benefit, Child Care Subsidy, Parental Leave Pay, Foster Child Health Care Card.

[136 150](tel:136150)

We may have sent your child a letter asking for this in September or October, read how you can [update your income details online](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/updating-parental-income-details).

# Your family income estimate
## Why we need a family income estimate
- [time limits for Child Care Subsidy](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/time-limits-for-confirming-income-for-child-care-subsidy).

- compare your family income estimate with your family’s actual [adjusted taxable income](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/what-adjusted-taxable-income?context=22151)

- family’s actual [adjusted taxable income](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/what-adjusted-taxable-income?context=41186) used to [balance your payments](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/balancing-your-family-assistance-payments).

## What to include in your family income estimate
You need to tell us about your and your partner’s [adjusted taxable income](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/what-adjusted-taxable-income?context=22151) for the whole financial year.

This should include both:

- any [taxable](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/paying-tax-centrelink-payment?context=22151) payments you get from us or the Department of Veterans’ Affairs
- certain [non-taxable Australian Government payments](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/what-adjusted-taxable-income?context=22151) you get from us or the Department of Veterans’ Affairs
- any child support or spousal maintenance you pay.

- [reportable fringe benefits](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/what-adjusted-taxable-income?context=22151#reportablefringebenefits), how we assess these depends on the type of employer you have
- [early released superannuation](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/early-release-superannuation), for any reasons except the First Home Super Saver Scheme

Any child support or spousal maintenance you receive may also affect the [amount of FTB you get](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/income-test-for-family-tax-benefit-part?context=22151#incometest).

## What not to include in your family income estimate
You don’t need to include [FTB](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/family-tax-benefit) or [CCS](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/child-care-subsidy).

- [Child support or spousal maintenance](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/income-test-for-family-tax-benefit-part?context=22151#incometest)
- [Carer Allowance](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/carer-allowance)

web.title: Consequences of having a reportable fringe benefits amount
web.description:
# Consequences of having a reportable fringe benefits amount
How your reportable fringe benefits amount affects eligibility and income tests for government benefits and obligations.

**Last updated** 5 June 2026

Print or Download

## How the reportable fringe benefits amount is used
Your [reportable fringe benefits amount (RFBA)](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/jobs-and-employment-types/working-as-an-employee/reportable-fringe-benefits-for-employees) is the 'grossed up' value of fringe benefits you received from your employer (or employers).

You aren't taxed on your RFBA. However, it's used to determine:

- your liability for the Medicare levy surcharge
- your child's [adjusted taxable incomeExternal Link](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/topics/what-adjusted-taxable-income/29571), which affects whether they are considered a dependant for Medicare levy purposes
- your entitlement to the private health insurance rebate
- whether you're liable for [Division 293 tax](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/super-for-individuals-and-families/super/growing-and-keeping-track-of-your-super/caps-limits-and-tax-on-super-contributions/division-293-tax-on-concessional-contributions-by-high-income-earners) for superannuation contributions
- your eligibility for the government co-contribution for personal super co-contributions you made
- your eligibility for the low-income super tax offset for [concessional](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/super-for-individuals-and-families/super/growing-and-keeping-track-of-your-super/caps-limits-and-tax-on-super-contributions/concessional-contributions-cap) (before tax) super contributions that you or your employer pay into your super fund
- whether you can offset your business loss against other income (non-commercial losses)
- if you're entitled to reduce your employee share scheme discount
- your entitlement to a tax offset for
  - contributions you made to your spouse's super
  - invalid and invalid carer
  - zone or overseas forces
  - Medicare levy surcharge (lump sum payment in arrears)
  - seniors and pensioners
- your eligibility for family assistance payments, including
  - Family Tax Benefit Part A and Part B
  - Child Care Subsidy (from 2 July 2018)
  - Parental Leave Pay
  - Dad and Partner Pay (prior to 30 June 2024)
- your child support obligations.

### Example: RFBA used to work out the amount of HELP to repay
Olivia estimates her taxable income will be $70,000 in 2025–26. Based on this taxable income, Olivia would have a compulsory HELP repayment of $450.

However, in 2025–26 Olivia also expects to receive fringe benefits from her employer with a reportable fringe benefit amount (RFBA) of $17,000. The RFBA isn't taxable, but it is added to Olivia's taxable income to determine her 'repayment income', which is the amount used to work out how much Olivia will need to repay towards her HELP debt.

If Olivia receives an RFBA of $17,000, then her HELP compulsory repayment estimate is worked out as:

Taxable income + RFBA

$70,000 + $17,000 = $87,000

This means Olivia would have a HELP [compulsory repayment](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-rates-and-codes/study-and-training-support-loans-rates-and-repayment-thresholds) of $3,000 for 2025–26.

End of example

### Example: RFBA used by Services Australia for Child Care Subsidy
Elijah's taxable income is $100,000 for the 2025–26 income year. Elijah's employer provides him with a car fringe benefit with a taxable value of $3,500. Elijah also receives a housing fringe benefit with a taxable value of $1,000. These fringe benefits are both reportable.

The taxable value of Elijah's fringe benefits is $3,500 + $1,000 = $4,500. The grossed-up taxable value of these benefits is $8,490 ($4,500 × 1.8868 (the lower gross-up rate for 2026)).

This means Elijah has a reportable fringe benefits amount (RFBA) of $8,490.

Elijah receives the Child Care Subsidy from Services Australia. When Services Australia works out how much Elijah is entitled to, they include both his taxable income and his RFBA:

$100,000 + $8,490 = $108,490

Services Australia will use the income amount of $108,490 to work out Elijah's CCS entitlement.

End of example
